The Ashwood Charter

An invented source document, written for a test fixture. Ashwood is not a real place and
the charter is not a real document; both exist only to give the corpus loader something
chapter-structured to chew on.

Chapter 1

The charter opens with a list of the people who signed it. Fourteen names are given, and
the order of them is the first thing any reader notices, because the miller is written
above the reeve and the reeve is written above the priest. Whoever drafted the list was
making an argument about who mattered in Ashwood, and the argument was about grain.

The second passage sets out the days on which the market may be held. Two days a week are
named, and a third is promised for the weeks after harvest. The clause is short, but it is
the clause that made the charter worth keeping, because a market day is a right that can
be counted and therefore a right that can be defended.

The third passage concerns the bridge. It says that the bridge belongs to nobody and that
everybody must maintain it, which sounds generous until the next sentence explains that
maintenance is owed in labour, three days a year, from every household that uses it. The
charter is at its plainest here, and at its least popular.

A fourth passage, added in a different hand, forbids the felling of the ash trees along
the river bank. No reason is recorded. Later readers have supplied several, none of which
can be checked against anything else in the document.

Chapter 2

The second half of the charter is a set of penalties, and it is much less careful than the
first. Fines are given in shillings for some offences and in days of labour for others,
with no rule offered for converting between them. A dispute about the conversion appears
in the margin, undated, in a third hand.

The penalty for blocking the market road is heavier than the penalty for striking a
neighbour. Readers meeting the charter for the first time usually find this shocking, and
it is worth sitting with the shock before explaining it away, because the explanation is
the whole point: the road was the town's income and the neighbour's bruises were not.

The closing passage promises that the charter will be read aloud twice a year in the
market square. That promise is the only mention of an audience anywhere in the text, and
it tells us the document was meant to be heard rather than consulted. Its short sentences
and repeated phrasings make sense once you read it out loud.

The charter ends without a date. Every claim about when it was written rests on the
handwriting, on the names in the opening list, and on the bridge, which is mentioned in
one other invented document and not in any real one.
